title: Post-Mortem: The Project That Failed
description: It is six months after the product launch. Sales are 80% below forecast. You are the project lead walking through what went wrong — not to assign blame, but to understand it. Rounds 1–5 trace five critical decisions backward. Rounds 6–10 ask what you would do differently, and what you are willing to commit to changing in yourself.
learning_concept: Failure is the richest learning environment available, but only if you approach it as a forensic investigation rather than a shame exercise. The difference between blame and accountability is not about softening the facts — it is about asking better questions. Systems produce outcomes. People make decisions inside systems. Understanding both is how organizations actually learn.
learning_objectives: Distinguish between blame (assigning fault to a person) and accountability (understanding how a decision was made and what made it likely)
Apply systems thinking to failure analysis — identifying the pressures, incentives, and information gaps that shaped each bad decision
Develop the capacity to hold yourself accountable for your own role without collapsing into shame or defensiveness
Understand how post-mortem analysis, done well, is one of the highest-value organizational learning activities available

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: It is six months after your product launch. Sales are 80% below forecast. You are the project lead.
Rounds 1–5 walk backward through five decisions that were made during the project. For each one, you identify the root cause of why that decision failed.
Rounds 6–10 move forward: you propose what you would do differently and commit to one specific behavioral change for each failure.
There is no 'winning' this game. There is only how honestly you are willing to engage with what happened and what you carry forward.

Track three resources: Accountability Score (how precisely you name your own role), Learning Depth (the sophistication of your failure analysis), and Systemic Understanding (how well you see the structural forces that shaped decisions).
tips: The hardest rounds are not the ones that identify what went wrong. They are the ones that ask what you would commit to changing in yourself.
Systemic pressures are real, but they do not remove individual accountability. Both are true at the same time.
The most valuable post-mortems name specific decisions and specific people — not to blame, but to be precise. Vague accountability is not accountability.
Notice when your explanations are moving toward justification rather than inquiry. That shift is the one to watch.

psychological_framework.description: This game draws on three bodies of research: Sidney Dekker's 'New View' of human error (humans make rational decisions given what they knew at the time), Chris Argyris's double-loop learning (questioning the assumptions behind decisions, not just the decisions themselves), and Amy Edmondson's work on psychological safety in organizational failure (teams that can discuss failure openly learn faster and perform better over time). The forensic tone of the game is intentional — curiosity, not judgment, is the tool.

core_skills.name: Resilience
core_skills.description: The capacity to face failure without collapse — to look at what went wrong with curiosity rather than shame, and to carry the learning forward rather than the injury.

core_skills.name: Strategic Thinking
core_skills.description: The ability to trace effects back to causes across complex systems — identifying not just what went wrong but the chain of pressures and decisions that made it likely.

core_skills.name: Adaptability
core_skills.description: Updating your mental models based on evidence from failure, rather than protecting previous beliefs about how the world works or how you behave.

core_skills.name: Delayed Gratification
core_skills.description: Resisting the urge to close the inquiry early with a simple explanation — staying in the discomfort of open questions long enough to reach a real understanding.

glossary_terms.definition: A systematic process for identifying the fundamental, underlying causes of an event or problem — as opposed to addressing only the surface symptoms.
glossary_terms.example: A bug in production is the symptom. The root cause might be a code review process that was skipped under deadline pressure — and the root cause of that is an incentive structure that rewards speed over quality.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: The classic RCA technique is the 'Five Whys' — asking 'why' five times in succession until you reach a causal layer that, if addressed, would prevent recurrence. Most organizations stop at why number two. The hard insight is that root causes are almost always systemic, not individual.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: After the Challenger disaster, NASA's initial investigation focused on the O-ring failure (symptom). The deeper root cause, identified by the Rogers Commission, was an organizational culture that suppressed safety concerns under schedule pressure — a systemic problem that existed years before the disaster.

glossary_terms.definition: The tendency to believe, after an event has occurred, that you would have predicted or prevented it — which distorts your analysis of whether a decision was actually bad at the time it was made.
glossary_terms.example: After a failed product launch, believing 'we should have known the market wasn't ready' — when the data available at the time genuinely supported the decision.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Hindsight bias is one of the most dangerous distortions in failure analysis. It makes bad decisions look like stupidity rather than rational choices under uncertainty. Sidney Dekker calls this 'substituting the outcome for the process' — judging a decision by how it turned out rather than by what a reasonable person would have decided given what was known.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Post-2008 financial crisis analyses routinely described the warning signs as 'obvious in retrospect.' Research by Nassim Taleb and others shows that the same data, presented prospectively, would not have generated the same level of certainty — the risk only looked inevitable after it materialized.

glossary_terms.definition: A form of organizational learning that questions the underlying assumptions and values that led to a decision, not just the decision itself. Contrasted with single-loop learning, which only asks 'how do we fix this?'
glossary_terms.example: Single-loop: 'We missed the launch deadline, so next time we will build more buffer into the schedule.' Double-loop: 'Why did we consistently underestimate how long things take? What does that reveal about our planning culture or our relationship to uncertainty?'
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Chris Argyris and Donald Schon developed double-loop learning theory to explain why organizations repeat the same mistakes even after fixing the surface problem. The answer: they address the symptom without questioning the mental models that generated it. Double-loop learning is uncomfortable because it requires examining assumptions that people often hold as unquestionable.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Toyota's famous production system is built on double-loop learning. The 'stop the line' principle means any worker can halt production when they see a problem — not to fix it (single-loop) but to understand why it happened (double-loop). This practice is a primary reason Toyota has one of the lowest defect rates in manufacturing.

halftime_config.reflection_question: You have traced five decisions backward through the failure. Before you move to what you would do differently: which of these five decisions feels most like yours — the one where your fingerprints are most clearly on the root cause?
halftime_config.custom_message: Act 2 begins now. You have identified what happened. The harder question is what to do with that knowledge.

rounds.title: Decision 5 Backwards: The Launch Date
rounds.story:
Six months ago, you launched Meridian — a B2B analytics platform — on October 14th. Sales are now 80% below the forecast of $2.4M ARR in year one. You are sitting in a conference room with your COO, your VP of Sales, and a blank whiteboard. The post-mortem has begun.

The first thing the whiteboard surfaces: the October 14th date. It was not your original date. The original date was December 1st — six weeks later. The date moved forward in late September because the CEO was presenting at a major industry conference on October 16th and wanted to be able to say 'we just launched' from the stage. The product was not fully ready. The onboarding flow had three known critical issues. The sales team had not completed their training. The first enterprise customer call happened forty-eight hours after launch — before the sales team knew the product well enough to demo it.

What was the root cause of the launch date decision?
rounds.goal: Identify the root cause of the premature launch date
rounds.coaching_moment: Naming the root cause of a failure is not the same as assigning blame. The CEO was not malicious. They were responding to a real incentive — a major stage, a visible moment, a competitive pressure. The question is: what in the system made that incentive strong enough to override product readiness?

choices.label: Root cause: insufficient process for challenging executive decisions on timelines
choices.feedback: This is a strong systemic root cause. When there is no formal process for a team to escalate 'this product is not ready for the proposed date' to executive decision-makers in a way that gets heard, the incentive to ship for optics will always override the evidence for delay. The CEO's conference stage reasoning made complete local sense — and the team had no mechanism to surface the global cost. The fix is structural, not interpersonal.
choices.coaching_moment: Systemic root causes are harder to name than personal ones, but they are more actionable. You cannot change someone's ambition. You can change the structures that either check it or amplify it.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This is a strong systemic root cause. When there is no formal process for a team to escalate 'this product is not ready for the proposed date' to executive decision-makers in a way that gets heard, the incentive to ship for optics will always override the evidence for delay.

choices.label: Root cause: the project lead (me) did not push back hard enough on the date change
choices.feedback: This answer carries real accountability and it is not wrong. There was a moment where you, as project lead, had the information and the standing to say: 'This launch date is not ready and here is exactly what will go wrong.' Whether you said it, how forcefully you said it, and what happened when you did — those are all part of the story. This root cause is honest. It is also incomplete if it stops here. Why did you not push back harder? That is the next why.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This answer carries real accountability and it is not wrong. There was a moment where you, as project lead, had the information and the standing to say: 'This launch date is not ready and here is exactly what will go wrong.

choices.label: Root cause: the organization had no shared definition of 'launch ready' — everyone was measuring different things
choices.feedback: This is a sophisticated and often overlooked root cause. When 'launch ready' means 'technically functional' to engineering, 'demos well' to sales, 'clears legal' to compliance, and 'has a press release' to marketing — you have a coordination failure waiting to happen. The CEO moved the date because, from their vantage point, the product was ready. From the onboarding engineer's vantage point, it was not. Both were using different definitions of the same word. The fix requires a shared artifact: a written, agreed-upon readiness checklist that every function signs off on before a date is confirmed.

rounds.reflection_prompt: Knowing the outcome, what pressure or incentive led to this launch date being chosen anyway?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Decision 4 Backwards: The Sales Forecast
rounds.story:
The $2.4M ARR forecast. Where did that number come from? You trace it back through the whiteboard. The sales team built a model based on a comparable product launch from eighteen months earlier — a different product, a different market segment, a faster growth environment. The head of sales presented the forecast at the board meeting with a confidence interval that was never written down. When the board asked 'how confident are you?', the answer was 'very' — which, it turns out, meant 'confident based on a model I believe in,' not 'confident based on independent validation.'

The forecast was never stress-tested. There was no downside case in the board presentation. No one asked 'what would have to be true for us to miss this by 50%?'. The board approved the go-ahead, the hiring plan, and the marketing budget based on a number that had no explicit confidence interval and no documented assumptions.

What was the root cause of the forecast failure?
rounds.goal: Identify the root cause of the inaccurate sales forecast
rounds.coaching_moment: Forecasting failures are almost always about the process around the forecast, not the forecast itself. A number without documented assumptions is a guess wearing a spreadsheet.

choices.label: Root cause: the board culture rewarded optimism and did not create space to challenge assumptions
choices.feedback: This is a genuine systemic root cause. In many organizations, presenting a pessimistic forecast is read as a lack of belief in the product or the team — which creates a social pressure toward optimism that corrupts the forecasting function entirely. The head of sales presented what the room wanted to hear, and the room rewarded them for it. The fix requires deliberate board culture work: requiring a written downside case, assigning a formal devil's advocate role in planning sessions, and treating pessimistic analysis as intellectual rigor rather than defeatism.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This is a genuine systemic root cause. In many organizations, presenting a pessimistic forecast is read as a lack of belief in the product or the team — which creates a social pressure toward optimism that corrupts the forecasting function entirely.

choices.label: Root cause: the forecast used a comparable that was not actually comparable
choices.feedback: This is a specific and accurate analytical root cause. The comparable product was in a faster-growing market, had different buyer personas, and launched into a different competitive environment. Using it as a benchmark without documenting those differences was an analytical error that anyone could have caught — if they had asked. The deeper question: why did no one ask? The forecast was not independently reviewed. There was no cross-functional validation step. The answer lived in a single team's model.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This is a specific and accurate analytical root cause. The comparable product was in a faster-growing market, had different buyer personas, and launched into a different competitive environment.

choices.label: Root cause: no one asked 'what would have to be true for us to miss this by 80%?'
choices.feedback: This is an excellent process-level root cause. The pre-mortem — invented by psychologist Gary Klein — is one of the most effective forecasting interventions available. It asks, before a decision is made: 'Imagine it is six months from now and this failed badly. What happened?' This question surfaces assumptions that would never emerge from a forward-looking planning exercise. The answer to 'why did no one ask this question' is almost always: because the organization does not have a habit of asking it. That habit can be built.
choices.coaching_moment: The pre-mortem is one of the most underused tools in strategic planning. It is not pessimism — it is the intellectual discipline of identifying your own blind spots before they become catastrophes.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What made the sales forecast feel believable at the time — and what would have made someone question it?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Decision 3 Backwards: The Customer Research
rounds.story:
Back further: four months before launch, your team conducted user research. Five interviews with potential customers. The research was conducted by two team members who were deeply invested in the product and believed in it strongly. The research findings document was twelve pages long. Page two contained, in a bullet point, a quote from one interviewee: 'I am not sure our procurement process would allow us to adopt a tool like this without a formal security audit.'

That bullet point was not in the executive summary. It was not discussed in the research readout meeting. It was not escalated. Six months later, your VP of Sales tells you that three of the four largest deals you lost cited 'security compliance concerns' as the primary reason for not proceeding.

What was the root cause of the customer research failure?
rounds.goal: Identify the root cause of missing the security compliance signal
rounds.coaching_moment: The signal was in the data. It was missed not because no one looked, but because of how humans process information that challenges beliefs they have already formed. This is not a failure of intelligence. It is a failure of process design.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think about a time when you had access to information that should have changed a decision — but did not. What was happening in you or in the room that allowed the signal to be recorded but not acted on?

choices.label: Root cause: confirmation bias — researchers who believed in the product minimized disconfirming findings
choices.feedback: Confirmation bias is a genuine and well-documented root cause of research failure. When the people conducting research have a strong prior belief, they are psychologically inclined to weight confirming evidence more heavily than disconfirming evidence — not dishonestly, but automatically. The fix is structural: independent research review, explicit 'devil's advocate' steps in the research synthesis process, and a requirement to surface the three most concerning findings before the executive summary. Research conducted by true believers needs extra scrutiny, not less.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Confirmation bias is a genuine and well-documented root cause of research failure. When the people conducting research have a strong prior belief, they are psychologically inclined to weight confirming evidence more heavily than disconfirming evidence — not dishonestly, but automatically.

choices.label: Root cause: insufficient research sample — five interviews cannot identify systemic buyer concerns
choices.feedback: A valid methodological root cause. Five interviews is a sufficient sample for exploring open questions, but a thin sample for validating or dismissing specific concerns. When one out of five interviewees raises a procurement/security issue, the right response is to probe further — talk to five more enterprise procurement officers, specifically about the security audit question. The signal was real; the response was under-resourced. The deeper question: why was the research budget this small for a decision of this magnitude?
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A valid methodological root cause. Five interviews is a sufficient sample for exploring open questions, but a thin sample for validating or dismissing specific concerns.

choices.label: Root cause: no process for escalating 'single mentions' that concern enterprise buyers specifically
choices.feedback: This is a sophisticated systemic root cause. The security audit concern appeared once in five interviews — which, by frequency, did not make it into the executive summary. But enterprise buyers are not like consumer users: a single procurement concern that one buyer surfaces is often a concern shared by all enterprise buyers, who simply may not have volunteered it unprompted. The research process did not have a special protocol for enterprise-specific structural concerns. One mention of 'our procurement process' from a single enterprise buyer is not a data outlier — it is a signal about an entire buying segment. The system needs to flag it differently.
choices.coaching_moment: In enterprise sales, the concerns that buyers raise unprompted — without being directly asked — are often more significant than the ones they raise in response to your questions. They volunteered that signal. The system was not designed to hear it.

expert_pick.reason: Experts recommend this approach for long-term growth.

rounds.title: Decision 2 Backwards: The Competitor Analysis
rounds.story:
Further back: eight months before launch, you completed a competitive analysis. Your deck identified three direct competitors and positioned Meridian as superior on four dimensions: reporting depth, real-time data refresh, UX quality, and pricing. The pricing claim was accurate. The UX quality claim was based on your own team's assessment. The reporting and refresh rate claims were based on competitor documentation that was, at the time, twelve to eighteen months old.

Three weeks before your launch, a competitor released a major product update that closed the reporting gap entirely. You learned about this from a sales prospect who mentioned it in passing during a demo. Your team had no competitive monitoring process. No one had set up alerts. No one had checked the competitor's changelog. The update had been publicly announced four weeks prior.

What was the root cause of the competitive intelligence failure?
rounds.goal: Identify the root cause of missing the competitor update
rounds.coaching_moment: Competitive analysis is not a document — it is a practice. A snapshot of the competitive landscape from eight months ago is not intelligence. It is history.

choices.label: Root cause: no one owned competitive monitoring as an ongoing responsibility
choices.feedback: This is the cleanest systemic root cause. Competitive analysis was treated as a project milestone rather than a function. When the deck was completed, the work was considered done — even though the competitive landscape continued to evolve. The fix is an ownership assignment: one person, explicitly accountable for competitive monitoring, with a monthly cadence and a structured output that goes to product and sales. 'Everyone is responsible' for competitive monitoring means 'no one is responsible.'
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This is the cleanest systemic root cause. Competitive analysis was treated as a project milestone rather than a function.

choices.label: Root cause: the analysis was built on outdated sources and no one validated the primary claims
choices.feedback: A specific and accurate analytical root cause. Competitive claims built on documentation from twelve to eighteen months ago in a fast-moving software market are not just stale — they are actively misleading. Any competitive claim used in a sales deck should be validated against the competitor's current product within thirty days of use. The team treated research quality as a one-time activity. In software, it is a continuous one.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A specific and accurate analytical root cause. Competitive claims built on documentation from twelve to eighteen months ago in a fast-moving software market are not just stale — they are actively misleading.

choices.label: Root cause: the team had no structured way to receive and process external signals — competitors, market, customers — between major milestones
choices.feedback: This is the deepest root cause — and the one that connects to the customer research failure in round 3, the forecast failure in round 2, and the launch date failure in round 1. The team was operating with an internally-facing planning process in an externally-changing environment. There was no structured practice for receiving, processing, and acting on signals from outside the project. The competitor update, the security concern from the customer interview, the changing market conditions — all of these were available. None of them had a channel into decision-making. This is an organizational learning architecture failure.
choices.coaching_moment: The best planning processes are porous — they have deliberate entry points for new information to reach decision-makers before it becomes a crisis. Most planning processes are hermetically sealed. This project was the latter.

rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do competitor signals so often get underweighted in real decisions? What cognitive bias is at work here?

expert_pick.reason: Experts recommend this approach for long-term growth.

rounds.title: Decision 1 Backwards: The Original Scope
rounds.story:
You have traced four failures. Now the furthest back: the original product scope. Twelve months before launch, you were in a product strategy session where the scope of Meridian was defined. The initial vision was a focused tool for one specific use case: automated reporting for mid-market SaaS companies. Clean, narrow, fast to build.

Over the next three months, four features were added to the scope in response to individual stakeholder requests. The VP of Enterprise Sales requested two enterprise-specific features. The CEO returned from a conference with a 'competitive intelligence' request that became a feature. A large potential customer in the pilot program asked for a custom data export format that became a product feature for everyone.

By the time development began, the scope was 60% larger than the original design. The timeline extended by three months. The build quality suffered. The onboarding flow — the first and most critical user experience — was rushed in the final weeks.

What was the root cause of the scope failure?
rounds.goal: Identify the root cause of the project's scope expansion
rounds.coaching_moment: Scope creep is never really about scope. It is about who has the power to add to scope, what the process is for evaluating additions, and whether the cost of each addition is made visible before it is agreed to.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What does the pattern across these five root causes tell you? Is there a single deeper failure underneath all of them — one thing that, if it had been different, might have changed the trajectory of this project?

choices.label: Root cause: no single owner of scope with the standing to say no to stakeholders
choices.feedback: This is the clearest structural root cause. When scope additions are made by individual stakeholders through informal conversations — without a product committee, without a cost-benefit analysis, without a formal change request — the project lead has no standing to decline. Every stakeholder believes their addition is the exception. The product lead needs both the structural authority and the organizational support to say: 'This is not in scope for this release. Here is the process to add it to the next one.' Authority without structure is easily overridden.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This is the clearest structural root cause. When scope additions are made by individual stakeholders through informal conversations — without a product committee, without a cost-benefit analysis, without a formal change request — the project lead has no standing to decline.

choices.label: Root cause: the scope additions were never costed — no one calculated the cumulative impact on timeline or quality
choices.feedback: A precise analytical root cause. Each scope addition was evaluated in isolation: 'Can we build this?' rather than 'What does adding this cost us across the entire project?' The answer to the second question — a three-month timeline extension, a 30% increase in build complexity, a compressed onboarding experience — would have changed the stakeholder calculus entirely. Most scope additions seem small. Their cumulative effect is what kills projects. The fix: any scope addition must include a full timeline and quality impact analysis before it is approved.
choices.coaching_moment: The cost of a scope addition is almost always a delayed cost — it shows up in build quality and timeline pressure months later, when the connection to the original decision is no longer visible.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A precise analytical root cause. Each scope addition was evaluated in isolation: 'Can we build this?' rather than 'What does adding this cost us across the entire project?' The answer to the second question — a three-month timeline extension, a 30% increase in build complexity, a compressed onboarding experience — would have changed the stakeholder calculus entirely.

choices.label: Root cause: the project had no explicit product vision that could be used as a filter for scope decisions
choices.feedback: This is the deepest root cause — and the one that connects most cleanly to the organizational learning architecture failure from round 4. The original product vision was 'automated reporting for mid-market SaaS.' But that vision was never written down, never shared as an explicit filter for decisions, and never used as a reference point when stakeholders arrived with additions. A clear product vision is a decision-making tool — it lets you say 'this feature request is outside our focus for this release' and have a principled reason, not just a capacity reason. Without it, every scope addition is evaluated on its own merits, and every stakeholder is the most convincing person in the room.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: What You Would Do Differently: The Launch Date
rounds.story:
You have traced all five failures backward. Now you move forward. The whiteboard has five root causes written on it. The question is no longer 'what happened?' — it is 'what would you commit to changing?'

Start with the launch date. The CEO wanted to say 'we just launched' from the conference stage. The product was not ready. You did not push back effectively. The system had no mechanism to surface product readiness concerns in a way that reached executive decision-makers.

If this happens again — and it will happen again, in some form — what do you commit to doing differently?
rounds.goal: Commit to a specific behavioral or structural change for the launch date failure
rounds.coaching_moment: A commitment to change is only as valuable as its specificity. 'I will push back harder next time' is not a commitment — it is a hope. A commitment names the specific behavior, the specific moment it applies to, and the specific cost you are willing to accept to do it.

choices.label: Build a formal launch readiness checklist with cross-functional sign-off — the date cannot move without everyone signing
choices.feedback: This is a structural commitment with teeth. The readiness checklist changes the social dynamic: instead of one person pushing back on an executive's preferred date, you have a shared artifact that the organization has already agreed represents the standard. 'The checklist is not complete' is a more durable resistance than 'I do not think we are ready.' You have moved the locus of accountability from one person's courage to a shared organizational agreement. This survives staff turnover and power dynamics better than any individual commitment can.

choices.label: Commit to writing a formal written objection when you believe a date decision is premature — on the record, with specifics
choices.feedback: This commitment is about personal accountability and professional courage. A written objection on the record — naming the specific risks, the specific unresolved issues, and your recommendation — is harder to dismiss than a verbal concern raised in a meeting. It also creates a paper trail: if the date moves and the product fails, the written objection demonstrates that the concern was surfaced and overruled, not missed. This commitment requires courage. It may not be popular. It is also the kind of behavior that, over time, builds a reputation for integrity that protects you and your team.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This commitment is about personal accountability and professional courage. A written objection on the record — naming the specific risks, the specific unresolved issues, and your recommendation — is harder to dismiss than a verbal concern raised in a meeting.

choices.label: Commit to requesting a joint meeting — project lead, CEO, and engineering lead — before any date change is finalized
choices.feedback: This commitment addresses the structural gap directly: date decisions happened without the engineering lead in the room. If the person who knows what is ready and what is not is present when the date is being set, the calculus changes. This is a process commitment that requires ongoing executive support to maintain — you cannot hold this meeting alone. Part of your commitment is advocating for it as a standard practice, not just requesting it on a case-by-case basis when you are worried.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This commitment addresses the structural gap directly: date decisions happened without the engineering lead in the room. If the person who knows what is ready and what is not is present when the date is being set, the calculus changes.

rounds.reflection_prompt: Now that you know what went wrong, what would have made the launch date decision look different at the time?

expert_pick.reason: Experts recommend this approach for long-term growth.

rounds.title: What You Would Do Differently: The Forecast
rounds.story:
The $2.4M ARR forecast. No confidence interval. No documented assumptions. No downside case. The board approved a hiring plan and a marketing budget based on a number that had never been stress-tested.

You were in the room when the forecast was presented. You did not ask for the downside case. You did not ask 'what would have to be true for us to miss this?' You were, honestly, also caught up in the optimism of the moment. The product felt ready. The market felt ready. The number felt right.

What do you commit to for the next forecast?
rounds.goal: Commit to a specific behavioral change for the forecasting failure
rounds.coaching_moment: Asking hard questions in a room where everyone is excited is one of the most difficult leadership moves. It requires tolerating being briefly seen as the person who lacks belief — in order to protect everyone from a more costly mistake later.

choices.label: Formally request a written downside case for any forecast over $1M — before board approval
choices.feedback: A clear, actionable structural commitment. The downside case is not pessimism — it is risk management. When the board sees both the optimistic and the realistic scenario, they make a more informed decision about the hiring plan and the marketing budget. The commitment to require it formally — as a board process, not a request you make when you feel uncertain — takes the social friction out of asking. It becomes a standard, not a challenge.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A clear, actionable structural commitment. The downside case is not pessimism — it is risk management.

choices.label: Assign a formal pre-mortem session before any major go/no-go decision — 'Assume it is six months later and we failed. What happened?'
choices.feedback: The pre-mortem is one of the highest-ROI planning interventions available. Research by Gary Klein and replicated many times since shows that teams that conduct pre-mortems identify significantly more risk factors than teams that use traditional risk assessment processes. The key insight: asking people to imagine failure has happened liberates them from the social pressure to appear optimistic — and activates a different type of thinking than prospective planning does. Committing to this as a standing practice, not a one-time exercise, is what makes it durable.
choices.coaching_moment: The pre-mortem works because it changes the frame from 'can we succeed?' to 'what exactly would failure look like?' The second question surfaces things the first one never reaches.

choices.label: Commit to asking 'what would have to be true for us to miss this by 50%?' in every major planning session you attend
choices.feedback: This is a personal behavioral commitment rather than a structural one — and it has a different character. You are committing to being the person who consistently asks the uncomfortable question, even when the room is excited. That role is genuinely valuable and genuinely uncomfortable. You will sometimes be seen as a skeptic. Over time, if you ask the question consistently and without personal agenda, you will be seen as the person who helps the team avoid expensive mistakes. That reputation takes time to build. It is built one uncomfortable question at a time.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This is a personal behavioral commitment rather than a structural one — and it has a different character. You are committing to being the person who consistently asks the uncomfortable question, even when the room is excited.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What story were you telling yourself about the forecast that allowed the optimism to persist this long?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: What You Would Do Differently: The Signals You Missed
rounds.story:
The security compliance concern in the customer research. The competitor update. Two external signals that were available and actionable — and that reached neither you nor the decision-making team in time to change anything.

You have traced the root causes: confirmation bias in the research process, no competitive monitoring function, no structured pathway for external signals to reach decision-makers. Now the commitment.

This is also the round where you have to be honest about something more personal: you had access to the research document. You read it. You did not see the security compliance bullet point, or if you did, it did not register as significant. What does that tell you about your own signal-processing in a context where you believed strongly in the product?
rounds.goal: Commit to a change that addresses how you personally process disconfirming information
rounds.coaching_moment: Structural fixes address the system. Personal commitments address the person inside the system. Both are necessary. A better research process would have helped. Your own confirmation bias would have still been present inside that better process.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What would you have needed in order to see that security compliance bullet point and treat it as significant, rather than a single data point among twelve pages? Was the problem in the document, in the process, or in how you were reading?

choices.label: Commit to reading customer research with a specific question: 'What in here, if true, would most damage our plan?'
choices.feedback: This is a personal cognitive commitment of real value. The question 'what in here most damages our plan?' is a frame-shift: you are not reading for confirmation, you are reading as an adversary. This mode of reading activates different attention. You are looking for vulnerabilities, not validations. It is uncomfortable to read your own team's work this way. It is also how you find the security compliance bullet point before it becomes a reason three enterprise deals fall through.
choices.coaching_moment: The frame you bring to a document determines what you see in it. Reading with confirmation bias is not a character flaw — it is a default. You can change the default by changing the question you bring.

choices.label: Build a structured competitive monitoring cadence — monthly review, owned by a named person, output goes to product and sales
choices.feedback: A structural commitment that directly addresses the competitive monitoring gap. The competitor update was in a public changelog. Someone with a monitoring responsibility and a monthly review cadence would have found it four weeks before you did. The commitment here is not just to build the process — it is to advocate for the resourcing and organizational standing it needs. A monitoring function that no one has time to run is not a function. It is an aspiration written on a whiteboard.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A structural commitment that directly addresses the competitive monitoring gap. The competitor update was in a public changelog.

choices.label: Commit to asking a colleague to specifically review your team's work for disconfirming evidence before major milestones
choices.feedback: This commitment addresses confirmation bias at its root: if your team is too invested to see the security compliance bullet point, find someone who is not invested and ask them to look specifically for problems. This is a form of red-teaming. It requires intellectual humility — you are inviting someone to find holes in your work — and a specific ask. 'Please review this for anything that concerns you' is too broad. 'Please read this research specifically looking for findings that would damage our launch plan' is the ask that gets you what you need.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This commitment addresses confirmation bias at its root: if your team is too invested to see the security compliance bullet point, find someone who is not invested and ask them to look specifically for problems. This is a form of red-teaming.

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: What You Would Do Differently: Scope Discipline
rounds.story:
The scope failures. Four features added after the initial design. No cost analysis. No shared product vision to filter against. An onboarding experience that was rushed because the earlier additions consumed the time and attention that the most important user-facing feature needed.

You have been the project lead on three products over the past four years. Looking back honestly, this is not the first time scope expanded beyond the original design. It happened on the second product too, though less severely. There is a pattern.

The pattern suggests that this is not just a process failure. It is something about how you relate to stakeholders, to requests, to the discomfort of saying no when someone with authority is asking for something.
rounds.goal: Commit to a behavioral change that addresses your role in scope expansion
rounds.coaching_moment: Process fixes are necessary but not sufficient when the pattern predates the current process. If scope expansion has happened twice across different projects, the common variable is not the process — it is the person operating inside the process.

choices.label: Commit to saying 'let me cost that' as an automatic response to every scope addition request — and sharing the cost before agreeing
choices.feedback: This is a behavioral script that creates a productive pause between request and agreement. 'Let me cost that' signals engagement without commitment. It creates a moment where the requester has to wait for information before the conversation can proceed. And when the cost analysis comes back — 'this feature will add three weeks to the timeline and push the onboarding work into the final sprint' — the requester now has the information they need to make a real decision rather than a wishful one. You are not saying no. You are saying: let us decide together with real information.

choices.label: Commit to naming the pattern to your manager — 'scope expansion is a recurring issue for me and I need structural support to address it'
choices.feedback: This is a high-accountability commitment and one of the hardest in the game. You are naming a personal pattern to someone who evaluates your performance. That requires real vulnerability. But it also creates accountability: your manager now knows, can watch for it, and can support you when a VP of Enterprise Sales arrives with a feature request that sounds reasonable and isn't. Naming your own pattern before someone else names it for you is a form of professional courage. It is also, strategically, how you get help.
choices.coaching_moment: The most effective way to change a persistent personal pattern is to make it visible to people who can observe it and help you catch it in real time. Accountability without witnesses is just intention.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This is a high-accountability commitment and one of the hardest in the game. You are naming a personal pattern to someone who evaluates your performance.

choices.label: Commit to building a product vision document at the start of every project and using it explicitly to filter scope additions
choices.feedback: A structural commitment that creates a standing reference point for scope decisions. When the CEO returns from a conference with a feature request, you can say: 'Here is our product vision for this release. Does this feature serve it? If yes, let us talk about the trade-off. If no, let us put it on the roadmap for the next version.' The vision document does not prevent scope additions — nothing does. But it gives you a principled, shared vocabulary for the conversation that is more durable than 'I do not think we have time.'
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A structural commitment that creates a standing reference point for scope decisions. When the CEO returns from a conference with a feature request, you can say: 'Here is our product vision for this release.

rounds.reflection_prompt: Scope discipline is easy in theory. What organisational or social pressures make it so hard in practice?

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Single Commitment
rounds.story:
The whiteboard has ten items on it. Five root causes traced backward. Five commitments made forward. The COO looks at you and says: 'If you had to pick one thing — one change to yourself or to how you run a project — that would have had the greatest impact on Meridian, what is it?'

This is not a rhetorical question. The answer you give will shape how the organization learns from this failure. It will shape what gets changed and what does not. It will also reveal something about how you have processed these two hours.

The COO is asking for a single commitment. What do you say?
rounds.goal: Name the single most important learning from the post-mortem
rounds.coaching_moment: The ability to identify the root of the root — the one insight that, if it had been present, would have changed the most downstream decisions — is the mark of a mature failure analyst. It requires holding the entire causal chain in your head and asking: where was the first moment where a different choice would have changed everything that followed?
rounds.reflection_prompt: Before you answer: what has this two-hour conversation surfaced that you were not expecting? Was there a moment where you felt the genuine discomfort of accountability — not guilt, but actual recognition that your specific choices contributed to a specific outcome? What was that moment?

choices.label: The single commitment: build and maintain a product vision document that every stakeholder has signed off on, and use it as the filter for every scope and timeline decision
choices.feedback: This commitment addresses the deepest structural failure: the absence of a shared north star for decision-making. The scope expansion happened because there was no agreed filter. The launch date moved because there was no shared definition of ready. The forecast went unchallenged because there was no shared standard for what 'conservative' meant. A product vision document is not a magic cure. But it is a shared language — and shared language is what makes it possible for a team to have real disagreements and make real decisions instead of defaulting to whoever has the most authority in the room.

choices.label: The single commitment: run a pre-mortem before every major go/no-go decision — imagine it is six months from now and we failed
choices.feedback: This commitment addresses the epistemic root cause: the team did not know what they did not know, and did not have a practice that would have surfaced it. The pre-mortem would have found the security compliance concern in the customer research. It would have challenged the forecast assumptions. It would have surfaced the risk of launching before the sales team was trained. One practice, applied consistently, catches the most dangerous category of error: the ones that feel obvious in hindsight and invisible in the moment. This is an elegant, high-leverage commitment.
choices.coaching_moment: The pre-mortem works because it makes it socially acceptable to be the person who imagines failure. Without it, imagining failure makes you the pessimist. With it, you are the rigorous thinker everyone wants on a launch team.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This commitment addresses the epistemic root cause: the team did not know what they did not know, and did not have a practice that would have surfaced it. The pre-mortem would have found the security compliance concern in the customer research.

choices.label: The single commitment: personally own the practice of surfacing disconfirming evidence — in every review, every research session, every forecast presentation
choices.feedback: This commitment is personal rather than structural — and it is the most self-aware one. You are naming that across every failure in this post-mortem, the common element was information that was available but not surfaced or acted on. The security concern was in the document. The competitor update was in a public changelog. The downside case was implicit in every optimistic assumption. You had access to all of this and you did not consistently ask for the disconfirming view. The commitment to become the person who always asks — not to be the skeptic but to be the rigorous thinker — is a leadership identity shift, not just a process change. That is the deepest commitment of the game.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This commitment is personal rather than structural — and it is the most self-aware one. You are naming that across every failure in this post-mortem, the common element was information that was available but not surfaced or acted on.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Tracing five failures backward without collapsing into blame or defensiveness
transfer_exercises.real_world: Think of a professional failure you have been avoiding examining closely. Write a five-why analysis: why did the outcome happen? Why did the decision that led to it happen? Keep going until you reach a level of cause that, if changed, would have changed the trajectory. Then write one specific thing you would commit to doing differently.
transfer_exercises.challenge: Share the analysis — or a version of it — with one colleague who was involved. Ask them: 'What root causes did I miss?' Notice what is uncomfortable about hearing their answer.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Using pre-mortem thinking to surface risks before they become failures
transfer_exercises.real_world: Before your next major decision or project milestone, run a five-minute pre-mortem: 'Assume it is six months from now and this failed badly. What happened?' Write down the three most plausible failure stories. Then ask: what can we do this week to make each of those stories less likely?
transfer_exercises.challenge: Propose a standing pre-mortem practice in your team's planning process. It does not need to be long — fifteen minutes before any major go/no-go decision. Notice what resistance the proposal meets, and what that resistance tells you about the team's relationship to discussing failure.

achievements.name: Forensic Analyst
achievements.description: In rounds 1–5, consistently chose root causes at the systemic level rather than the individual blame level — demonstrating an understanding that failures emerge from systems, not just people.

achievements.name: The Commitment
achievements.description: In rounds 6–10, made specific, behavioral commitments rather than vague intentions — demonstrating the difference between genuine accountability and performative self-criticism.

achievements.name: Accountability Without Shame
achievements.description: Finished the game with Accountability Score above 70 while maintaining Learning Depth above 70 — holding yourself accountable with precision without collapsing into blame or defensiveness.

cultural_context: Strategic thinking games have deep roots in Indian culture — from ancient Chaturanga (the predecessor of chess) to modern competitive gaming. Post-Mortem: The Project That Failed develops long-range planning and pattern recognition prized in Indian academic and professional settings.
coaching_moment: Every choice shapes your strategy — great leaders think several steps ahead before deciding.

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 5 rounds of Post-Mortem: The Project That Failed. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

hallmarks: Stabilizes the system before perfecting the analysis
Holds blameless framing under pressure — describes systems, not scapegoats
Publishes the full RCA when accountability requires it, not just convenience
Distinguishes between recurrence (system failure) and one-off (unlucky variance)
Lets data write the postmortem, not the loudest exec in the room
Names the on-call engineer to make the meeting end faster
Treats postmortem as PR exercise, not learning artifact
Compromises on root-cause depth to avoid uncomfortable findings
Lets the loudest stakeholder determine what gets published
Confuses incident closure with incident learning
